text:
AHNS (AAAI 2024) uses a random candidate pool, then selects a negative near a positive-dependent target score. Its criteria: positive-aware hardness, lower negative hardness for higher-scoring positives, and adjustable difficulty. A fixed pool-rank band therefore does not reproduce AHNS: rank alone ignores the positive score and changing score gaps. AHNS supports testing target-relative hardness rather than assuming higher-ranked negatives always help. [Paper](https://www.comp.hkbu.edu.hk/~lichen/download/AAAI24_Lai.pdf)

R2NS (WWW 2026) supports stochastic selection within a hard subset, but adds uniform-sampling warm-up, global approximate retrieval plus random candidates, and a progressively shrinking top-M selection range. It explicitly warns that small random pools yield fluctuating hardness and limited catalog coverage. Thus, random-pool rank bands are a plausible simplified experiment, not equivalent to R2NS; neither paper establishes gains for this NextItNet benchmark. [Paper](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf)

Suggested diagnostics and safeguards: record positive-minus-negative score margins, fraction of negatives outranking positives, pairwise loss/gradient magnitude, selected ranks, unique-item coverage, and training-frequency distributions versus uniform sampling. Measure score–popularity correlation and validation HR@10 by target popularity to detect shortcuts. Exclude padding, the current target, and observed training positives; warm up uniformly, randomize selection, and compare moderate bands against hardest-only sampling. Unobserved preference means false-negative rates cannot be measured directly here; popularity and title similarity are risk indicators, not labels. Select using the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10, keeping one trained NextItNet model per category.
